steps.name: outline
steps.narration: A rectangle measuring twenty-three by fourteen has area twenty-three groups of fourteen. We will prove that by splitting the sides.
steps.prompt: What does the area of the full rectangle represent?

steps.name: partition
steps.narration: Split twenty-three into twenty and three. Split fourteen into ten and four. Every part of both original side lengths is still present.
steps.prompt: Why must each side add back to its original length?

steps.name: part-1
steps.narration: Twenty times ten makes two hundred in the top-left region. That is the first partial product.
steps.prompt: Why is this part two hundred?

steps.name: part-2
steps.narration: Three times ten makes thirty in the top-right region. This width is three, not twenty-three.
steps.prompt: Which two side parts made thirty?

steps.name: part-3
steps.narration: Twenty times four makes eighty in the bottom-left region. We have not lost the four units from the height.
steps.prompt: Where does the eighty come from?

steps.name: part-4
steps.narration: Three times four makes twelve in the bottom-right. All four parts now fill the original rectangle.
steps.prompt: Have we counted every region exactly once?

steps.name: partials
steps.narration: Add two hundred, thirty, eighty and twelve. Every partial product is area, so the sum is the whole area.
steps.prompt: How does addition rebuild the whole rectangle?

steps.name: total
steps.narration: Two hundred plus thirty plus eighty plus twelve is three hundred and twenty-two. So twenty-three times fourteen is three hundred and twenty-two.
steps.prompt: How do you know no part was missed?

F704_STEPS.name: outline
F704_STEPS.narration: Three lots of the whole bracket x plus two. The outside three must multiply every part inside, not just x.
F704_STEPS.prompt: Which two lengths are inside the bracket?

F704_STEPS.name: partition
F704_STEPS.narration: Split the width into one x section and a two-unit section. The rectangle is three units high all the way across.
F704_STEPS.prompt: Does the three apply to both widths?

F704_STEPS.name: part-1
F704_STEPS.narration: The first area is three times x. That makes three x, because x is an unknown length.
F704_STEPS.prompt: Why is the left area three x?

F704_STEPS.name: part-2
F704_STEPS.narration: The second area is three times two, which is six. Both regions belong to the same rectangle.
F704_STEPS.prompt: What is three multiplied by two?

F704_STEPS.name: partials
F704_STEPS.narration: Add the two areas: three x plus six. We cannot combine them because three x and six are unlike terms.
F704_STEPS.prompt: Should we combine three x and six?

F704_STEPS.name: total
F704_STEPS.narration: The distributive law is proven: three times open bracket x plus two close bracket equals three x plus six. Multiply everything inside the bracket.
F704_STEPS.prompt: How can you check both parts were multiplied?

F705_STEPS.name: outline
F705_STEPS.narration: We have two brackets: x plus three and x plus two. The rectangle stands for their product, not just their sum.

F705_STEPS.name: partition
F705_STEPS.narration: Put x and three across the top. Put x and two down the side. The four intersections each need their own product.
F705_STEPS.prompt: How many small products will we make?

F705_STEPS.name: part-1
F705_STEPS.narration: First: x times x gives x squared. It has its own square region.
F705_STEPS.prompt: Why is x times x x squared?

F705_STEPS.name: part-2
F705_STEPS.narration: Next: three times x gives three x. The top right region accounts for this cross term.

F705_STEPS.name: part-3
F705_STEPS.narration: Then: two times x gives two x. This is another cross term, and we must not miss it.
F705_STEPS.prompt: What happens to the second x term?

F705_STEPS.name: part-4
F705_STEPS.narration: Finally: two times three gives six. We have multiplied every term in one bracket by every term in the other.
F705_STEPS.prompt: Where does the six come from?

F705_STEPS.name: partials
F705_STEPS.narration: Both cross terms contain x. Add three x and two x to make five x, but do not combine x squared with x.
F705_STEPS.prompt: Which two terms are like terms?

F705_STEPS.name: total
F705_STEPS.narration: So the expanded expression is x squared plus five x plus six. The four regions prove it is equivalent to the original two brackets.
F705_STEPS.prompt: How does each region support the final expression?

steps.name: ends
steps.prompt: Which two whole numbers always multiply to the target?
steps.narration: Begin with one and twenty-four. Every positive whole number is divisible by one, so one times twenty-four equals twenty-four.

steps.name: outer
steps.prompt: Where do the ends of the widest arch land?
steps.narration: Draw one arch from one to twenty-four. Its two endpoints multiply to twenty-four.

steps.name: two
steps.prompt: Does twenty-four divide evenly into groups of two?
steps.narration: Two times twelve is twenty-four. Add the next factor arch, linking two and twelve.

steps.name: three
steps.prompt: Which partner belongs with three?
steps.narration: Three times eight is twenty-four. Draw an inner arch for this exact pair.

steps.name: four
steps.prompt: Why are the endpoints moving closer together?
steps.narration: Four times six is twenty-four. As one factor increases, its partner decreases.

steps.name: fail
steps.prompt: Is five a factor of twenty-four? Explain the remainder.
steps.narration: Five cannot divide twenty-four exactly. Four groups of five leave four, so five is not a factor.

steps.name: root
steps.prompt: Why can we stop after four?
steps.narration: The square root of twenty-four lies between four and five. Any factor bigger than this has a smaller partner already checked.

steps.name: proof
steps.prompt: List every factor without duplicating a partner.
steps.narration: The factors of twenty-four are one, two, three, four, six, eight, twelve and twenty-four. They divide exactly. Multiples of twenty-four begin twenty-four, forty-eight and seventy-two.

steps.name: Start with one and two
steps.narration: A prime is a whole number greater than one with exactly two positive factors. One is not prime. Two is the first prime.

steps.name: Circle two
steps.narration: Circle two: it is prime. All other even numbers are multiples of two and will be removed.

steps.name: Cross multiples of two
steps.narration: Cross out four, six, eight and all the other multiples of two. Leave two standing, because two itself is prime.

steps.name: Cross multiples of three
steps.narration: The next uncrossed number is three. It is prime. Cross its multiples starting at nine; six was already crossed by two.

steps.name: Cross multiples of five
steps.narration: Five is the next uncrossed prime that still has new composite multiples to eliminate. Begin at twenty-five.

steps.name: Cross multiples of seven
steps.narration: Seven is the final needed sieve prime up to one hundred. Cross multiples beginning at forty-nine. Every remaining number above one is prime.

steps.name: Start a factor tree
steps.narration: Switch to a factor tree for sixty. A composite number can be divided into two smaller whole-number factors.

steps.name: Split into six and ten
steps.narration: Sixty can be split into six times ten. This is an exact product, but both branches are still composite.

steps.name: Split six and ten
steps.narration: Split six into two and three, and ten into two and five. The leaves are all prime numbers.

steps.name: Collect prime factors
steps.narration: The prime factorisation of sixty is two times two times three times five, or two squared times three times five. Multiplying the leaves must recover the starting number.

steps.name: Begin with sixty
steps.narration: Prime factorisation means writing sixty as a multiplication of prime numbers. We start with sixty at the top of the division ladder.

steps.name: Divide by two
steps.narration: Two is the smallest prime divisor of sixty. Sixty divided by two is thirty. We write two on the left and thirty on the right.

steps.name: Divide by two again
steps.narration: Thirty is still divisible by two. Divide thirty by two and write fifteen on the next rung.

steps.name: Divide by three
steps.narration: Fifteen is no longer divisible by two. Three is its smallest prime divisor, giving five.

steps.name: Finish with five
steps.narration: Five is prime. Divide five by five to reach one. The prime ladder is complete only when the final quotient is one.

steps.name: Collect the prime divisors
steps.narration: Read the prime numbers in the left column: two, two, three and five. Multiplying them gives sixty.

steps.name: Write index form
steps.narration: Two appears twice, so write two squared. Three and five each appear once. Sixty equals two squared times three times five.

steps.name: Expand the first power
steps.narration: An index counts repeated factors of the same base. Two cubed means two multiplied by two multiplied by two. Expand each power so every factor can be seen.

steps.name: Join the factor strips
steps.narration: Both powers share the base two. Join the three factors to the two factors. This gives five factors of two without changing the multiplication.

steps.name: Recount the factors
steps.narration: Count the joined factors carefully. There are five factors, not six. With the same base, adding powers counts the factors.

steps.name: Compress into an index
steps.narration: Five factors of two can be written as two to the power of five. We keep the base and add the indices.

steps.name: Apply the law
steps.narration: For multiplication with the same base, a to the power of m times a to the power of n is a to the power of m plus n. We have proved this by counting the factors.

steps.narration: We know the area is fifty square units. We need the side length that would make a square with that area.

steps.name: Grow the side
steps.narration: Try a side length of five. Five times five gives twenty-five, so the square is too small.

steps.name: Test an overshoot
steps.narration: Try a side length of eight. Eight times eight is sixty-four, which is more than fifty. We have gone too far.

steps.name: Find both bounds
steps.narration: Seven squared is forty-nine and eight squared is sixty-four. The square root of fifty lies between seven and eight.

steps.name: Make a better estimate
steps.narration: Adjust the side to about seven point one. This gives an area close to fifty. The estimate is sensible because it lies between seven and eight.

steps.name: Start with an exact area
steps.narration: The area is seventy-two square units. Its side length is the square root of seventy-two, an exact value.

steps.name: Factorise the number
steps.narration: Seventy-two is thirty-six multiplied by two. Thirty-six is the largest perfect-square factor of seventy-two.

steps.name: Lift the square factor
steps.narration: We can separate the square-root expression into the square root of thirty-six multiplied by the square root of two.

steps.name: Take the exact square root
steps.narration: The square root of thirty-six is six. The square root of two remains exact; we do not replace it with a rounded decimal.

steps.name: Write simplest surd form
steps.narration: The square root of seventy-two equals six square root two. The number under the root no longer contains a square factor greater than one.
